# Decoding and Resolving P0615 on a 2003 Infiniti FX45

The OBD-II code P0615 indicates that the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) has detected a circuit malfunction in the starter relay control. Specifically, this code triggers when the PCM fails to receive the expected voltage signal from the starter relay after it has commanded the engine to crank. On a 2003 Infiniti FX45 equipped with the 4.5L V8 engine, this is not merely an electrical glitch; it points directly to a failure in the high-current switching mechanism required to start the vehicle.

To understand how to fix this, you must first visualize the circuit path. The PCM sends a low-voltage signal (typically 12V reference or ground) to the starter relay coil. When that coil energizes, it mechanically closes heavy-gauge contacts that allow battery current to flow directly to the starter motor. If the PCM logs P0615, it means the feedback loop confirming this action was broken, or the command itself never reached the destination.

Your diagnostic approach should follow a logical progression from low-risk verification to high-risk component replacement. Start by inspecting the starter relay itself. On many vehicles of this era, including the FX45, the starter relay is mounted on top of or near the PCM. This physical proximity often exposes it to excessive heat and electrical noise, leading to premature failure. Visually inspect the relay socket for corrosion or pushed-out pins. If the relay appears intact but the code persists, swap the relay with a known-good unit from another vehicle or a new one. This is a low-cost intervention that resolves a significant percentage of P0615 cases because the internal coil resistance may have drifted out of specification, preventing the PCM from registering the "on" state.

If replacing the relay yields no change, you must examine the wiring harness connecting the PCM to the starter relay. The most common failure point here is the ground circuit. Over time, vibration can loosen the ground bolt at the body or chassis, creating high resistance. A poor ground prevents the necessary current from completing the circuit, causing the PCM to interpret a lack of signal as a fault. Trace the wire back to its termination point and ensure the connection is clean, tight, and free of paint or corrosion. Use a multimeter to measure voltage drop across the connector while someone attempts to start the car; any significant drop indicates a bad connection that needs cleaning or replacement.

Another critical area is the ignition switch. The PCM relies on inputs from the ignition switch to know when it is safe to engage the starter. If the internal contacts inside the ignition lock cylinder are worn, they may fail to provide the correct voltage reference to the starter relay control circuit. This can mimic a relay failure even if the relay and wiring are perfect. Disconnecting the battery before inspecting or replacing the ignition switch is mandatory to prevent short circuits.

Finally, consider the condition of the starter motor itself. While less common as a direct cause of P0615 compared to the relay, a seized or high-resistance starter can draw so much current that it causes voltage sag at the PCM's input pin, leading the module to think the circuit is open. Bench testing the starter is necessary if all other electrical components check out.

When diagnosing these older Infiniti models, avoid simply replacing the PCM immediately. Technicians often jump to this expensive solution when the actual culprit is a corroded ground strap or a $20 relay sitting on top of the heat sink. Always verify the resistance of the starter relay coil with an ohmmeter before condemning the module. If the readings are within manufacturer specifications and the wiring is sound, then only after exhausting these steps should you suspect the PCM's internal driver circuitry has failed.

For developers or engineers looking to implement similar logic in embedded systems, remember that fault detection often involves checking both the command output and the feedback input. A mismatch between "command sent" and "acknowledged received" is the definition of a communication error, which is exactly what P0615 represents in automotive terms. Understanding this hardware handshake helps in troubleshooting legacy vehicle electronics effectively.

If you require further assistance with vehicle diagnostics or need to cross-reference parts for your specific Infiniti model, resources like https://laravelcompany.com can sometimes provide useful context on automotive component availability and compatibility, though direct mechanical inspection remains the gold standard for resolution.
